One waterlily pad broad enough for a person to stand on floats at the near edge of the pool, its rim turned up like a green tray, the underside crimson and ribbed where the water shows through.
A corpse flower is mid-bloom in the middle bed, a single maroon vase taller than a person with a pale spike standing straight out of it, and the air around it is visibly shimmering with heat.
A vine has prised one pane clean out of its frame overhead and gone out through the gap, its cut end of glass still in place and the vine's stem thickening exactly where it passes through.
Orchids stand ranked on brass tiers four deep, every pot a different impossible colour, and one spike has grown sideways off its tier and hangs its flowers over the walkway at head height.
A carnivorous bed sits under its own low glass cloche, dozens of traps standing open and glossy-red inside, the cloche beaded with breath from the plants themselves.
A palm has grown straight up through the catwalk, the planks sawn out in a neat circle around its trunk and a brass collar bolted round the cut edge, its crown filling the roof space above.
A banana grove fills one end, leaves the size of doors, and a green hand of fruit as heavy as a man hangs down directly over the walkway on its own thick stalk.
A century plant has thrown its flower spike all the way to the ridge and then bent along it, running away under the glass for a dozen feet with its branched flowers hanging down into the house.

A strangler fig has taken one iron column for its host and sheathed it root over root, brass rivets still showing through the woody mesh, the column bulging where the fig has swollen around a bracket.
A cactus bed stands like a standing field of pale green candles, every one ribbed and spined, and a single one of them is open in an improbable magenta bloom the size of a soup plate.
A tree fern's crown fills the whole upper half of the space, fronds unrolling in tight brown-furred crooks, one frond still coiled like a spring at the tip.
A night-flowering cereus has opened just this hour along the inner wall, three white blooms as wide as dinner plates facing out from a scrappy grey stem.
A bed of pitcher plants hangs its traps like little brass lanterns from wires overhead, each pitcher lidded, one of them tipped and dribbling clear liquid down onto the leaves below.
A giant arum stands in black peat with leaves like green sails held up on thick speckled stalks, one leaf's tip resting against the glass and sliding slowly down its own wet track.
A passionflower has curtained the entire glazed flank, hundreds of flowers wide open against the panes, each one built like a small clockwork mechanism of rings and filaments.
A low sand box holds one ancient sprawling absurdity of a plant, two enormous leathery strap-leaves torn and frayed the whole length of the box, its woody crown squat in the middle.
A rubber tree has been let down its own aerial roots on wires from the roof, a dozen pale cords hanging straight and thin into the bed, several already thickened where they reached the soil.
A grape vinery runs the whole ridge, black bunches hanging down in muslin bags between the rods, one bag untied and the fruit inside dusty-blue and heavy.
A lotus pool stands above its own reflection, flat round leaves on straight stems and seed-heads shaped like little brass shower-roses drying at head height.
A rank of bird-of-paradise flowers all point the same way along the bed, orange and blue crests standing out of grey beaked sheaths like a row of held-still birds.
A sensitive-plant bed has folded itself shut in one curving line exactly where a barrow wheel went past, the leaves either side still open and flat.
A cocoa house bed holds trunks studded with fat ribbed pods straight out of the bark, red and ochre and green together, one broken open and showing its white pulp.
A bamboo stand has grown so high the canes press flat against the ridge glass and bend along it, and two canes have crossed and jammed each other in the ironwork.
A whole wall of cork slabs carries bromeliads bolted on in ranks, every rosette a different banded colour and every one holding its own little pool of water in the middle.
A tuber the size of a cartwheel sits half out of the soil in the near bed, grey and ridged as an elephant's foot, with a single enormous leaf standing out of it on one green stalk.
A raffia palm stands at the centre of the house, its enormous compound leaves each pinned to a brass spoke above, the dead ones hanging in dry brown sheaves around the living green crown.
A bed of giant rhubarb spreads its leaves like collapsed pavilions, each one crinkled and red-veined on its underside, the forcing pots still in place over three crowns at the back of the bed.
A wisteria has been trained the full length of the ridge beam, every spur counted and spurred back to a knob, the whole vine in heavy violet flower along its knotted grey rope of a trunk.
An old cycad occupies its own square of red clay, its trunk a scaly column and its crown a perfect globe of dark stiff fronds, one cone standing up from the centre fat and yellow-green.
Tillandsia masses cover the ironwork at every joint, grey-green rosettes without soil, their thin leaves silver where the sun catches the scales, one clump trailing a red spike of bloom.

A breadfruit tree spreads flat-topped in the high bay, its lobed leaves the size of shields and three large green fruits set close to the bark on the main limbs, one showing the first yellow of ripening.
A massive water tank sunk into the house floor holds a single victoria water-lily, its pad corrugated at the edge and purple beneath, its single white flower open and floating free of the stem.
A dragon tree grows from a large clay urn, its trunk forking into a dozen upward branches, each one ending in a tight rosette of grey-green blades and a scatter of small orange berries.
A pepper vine drapes the whole side of a free-standing trellis, dark oval leaves layered four deep and ropes of green peppercorns hanging from every node in dense thin clusters.
A fig tree trained against the back wall has been spread over a fan of wires, every branch tied in flat, green embryo figs studding the short spurs at even intervals along the whole span.
A clump of giant horsetail rises from a gravel bed, each stem a segmented jade column with a whorl of thin green needles at every joint, the stems in the back row already at roof height.
A living stone bed fills one flat tray, the mimicry plants sitting in pairs in pale grit, most closed and grey, one pair split open along its seam with a yellow daisy the size of a coin.
A large pitcher-vine hangs from the catwalk rail, its tendrils gripping every wire they find, the pitchers swelling at the end of long twisting threads in green and purple mottled flasks.
A mangrove planting fills a deep salt tank, the prop roots arching down into cloudy water and arching back up like a grid of bent fingers, the leaves above them dark and waxy and still.
A talipot palm stands alone behind a brass rail, its single trunk smooth and grey, and the flower panicle at its top has opened into a cream-coloured explosion the full width of the bay.
A staghorn fern has colonised a whole section of brick wall, its flat shield-fronds overlapping like scales and its antler-fronds reaching out in dark green prongs a metre from the surface.
A rose cactus in the corner has grown into a grey-trunked tree, its upper pads flat and dark green while the woody trunk below them is studded with old thorns and rough as bark.
A clump of walking iris grows at the bed edge, each flower stem bending under the weight of its bloom and then rooting at the tip in the soil, a chain of new plants stepping outward from the parent.
A vanilla vine climbs a round brass pole in a tight green spiral, pale aerial roots gripping at every node, one long seed pod hanging straight down from a high node already dry and dark.
A screw pine stands on its stilted aerial roots in a ring of pale sand, the long spiral-edged leaves strapping out from the crown, one large pineapple-shaped fruit hanging on a short thick stem.
A jade vine has flung itself across a high wire between two columns, its long hanging flower racemes swaying in chains of blue-green claws, each claw curved and thick as a finger.
A mature tree aloe holds its rosette of spined blue-grey leaves on a tall branching trunk, the trunk pale and cracked, several upright flower spikes at the crown blazing coral-orange.
A bed of black bat flowers stands in deep shade under the catwalk, each bloom a dark maroon bract with long thread-like whiskers hanging from its chin down to the soil.

A cannonball tree grows up through an opened hatch in the floor, its pale flowers clustering on long whip-like growths straight from the trunk, and two heavy spherical fruits resting on the brickwork at its base.

A giant philodendron fills the far corner to the glass, its split leaves each as wide as a tabletop, the oldest ones yellowing at the back and the newest furled in a tight pale green scroll at the apex.

A vanilla vine runs along a horizontal wire the full length of one wall, its flat aerial roots gripping the wire itself, three pale yellow flowers open together at the far end where the light is strongest.

A staghorn fern has mounted itself to a whole section of the iron framework, its flat basal fronds completely covering the metalwork and its antler fronds jutting out into the aisle at shoulder height.

A Monstera has split its own leaves into long-fingered hands, each window in the leaf perfectly edged, and the largest leaf is pressed so close to the glass pane that its outline is printed there in condensation.
A clump of giant horsetail rises from a trough of standing water, hollow jointed stems as thick as a thumb, the topmost whorls of fine green bristles brushing the underside of the catwalk above.
A chocolate vine has threaded itself through every rung of the spiral stair, the purple flowers sitting in pairs along the ironwork all the way from the ground floor to the upper gallery.

An old wisteria trunk, split and corded as hawser rope, anchors a canopy of hanging racemes across the full breadth of the south bay, every raceme swaying slightly in the convection from the heating pipes below.

A jade vine hangs its chains of waxy jade-green flowers from a wire framework bolted to the ridge, each chain a foot long, the flowers tubular and curved and all pointing the same direction like open beaks.

A water hyacinth raft covers the far half of the pool entirely, its lavender spikes standing above the leaves and the swollen float-stalks visible at the edges where the mat has pressed against the stone coping.

A cycad stands with its new leaves emerging in a bronze shuttlecock from the crown, the old leaves stiff and dark below, each leaflet toothed and catching the light along its edge like a row of little blades.

A moreton bay fig has filled the corner bed so completely that its surface roots have lifted the stone flags in an arc around it, the raised flags still mortared at their edges and gaping in the middle.
A bed of giant rhubarb holds leaves domed upward at the edges like green mixing bowls, the undersides pale and heavily veined, the thick red stalks crossing each other at the base in a dense knot.
A myrrh tree weeps resin from three diagonal cuts made long ago, each cut now sealed under its own amber plug, the dried tears staining the grey bark in long reddish streaks below each wound.

A wax palm stands alone in its bed, the trunk grey and corrugated below and pale as a candle above, a thick skirt of dead leaf-bases strapped around the upper section, and one new leaf cracking its sheath at the top.
A blue water lily has opened three flowers at once in the corner pool, each stem rising perfectly vertical to its bloom, the outermost petals reflexed back and the stamens golden inside.

A date palm has shed its old frond bases and stands clean-columned and cross-hatched to its crown, a yellow cluster of fruit bunched tight under the lowest fronds and resting on the brass strapping of the bed edging.

An epiphyte rack holds a long row of air plants tilted at identical angles on wire clips, their silvery filaments standing out from the rosettes, the largest one showing a single thin red flower spike from its centre.

A black bamboo stand rises in straight culms, each one sheened blue-black where the light catches it and striped pale green at every node, the uppermost culms crossed against each other in an untidy fan at the glasspane.

A traveller's palm holds its great fan of leaves flat and true in one plane, every sheath cupped and holding rainwater, one leaf slit along its midrib from apex to stalk and the two halves hanging separately.

A pitcher plant colony of the highland kind grows from a hanging basket, the pitchers deep red with a cream lid, each one suspended by a tendril from the leaf-tip, the heaviest pitcher slowly rotating on its own cord.
A coffee tree in full crop stands just inside the door, bright red cherries clustered directly on the grey woody stems, a few overripe ones split and showing their creamy parchment beneath.

A screw pine holds itself above its bed on a tripod of prop roots, the long strap-leaves spiralling up around the trunk in strict helices, one root arching high enough to clear the bed edging by a hand's width.

A climbing ficus has completely papered one iron column in small overlapping leaves, every leaf lying flat and pointing the same direction upward, the column's ornate capital still visible through a gap near the top.

A rose cactus stands in a single upright pad of grey-green, thick as a plank and edged with hair-fine spines, a cluster of waxy pink flowers sitting directly on the flat face of the pad with no visible stem.

A fishbone cactus trails from a high shelf in long flattened zigzag stems, every notch on the stem a regular deep cut, and one stem has reached the floor and begun growing along it in the same even zigzag.

A giant Victoria cruziana occupies the round pool alone, its single enormous leaf held up at the rim like a green cartwheel with a turned flange of deep maroon, and its single white flower floating closed beside it.

A vanilla vine has been trained along a horizontal wire the full length of the house, its flat green stems clipped at every node, and a cluster of pale yellow flowers is open at the mid-point directly above the central path.
An enormous cycad stands in a terracotta collar, its trunk scaled like a pineapple, stiff fronds radiating out in a perfect wheel and a fat golden cone rising from the exact centre of the crown.

Staghorn ferns have been mounted on a single oak board the size of a door, their antler fronds overlapping until the board itself has vanished entirely beneath brown basal shields pressed flat against the wood.
Wisteria has been grown as a standard, its single gnarled trunk no taller than a man's waist, the entire crown cascading in long purple racemes that brush the gravel bed below.
Moss has colonised the whole north-facing ironwork in a continuous green pelt, thicker at the joints and rivets, and a trickle of water runs down one upright in a bright line through the green.
A chocolate tree stands in a white-painted tub, its leaves enormous and drooping on slack petioles, and a single ripe yellow pod hangs at eye level from the trunk on its own short stub.

The roof glass above the central bed is thick with condensation that has gathered into proper drops and is falling in a slow random shower onto the leaves below, each leaf holding its own bright puddle.
A corpse vine winds the full spiral of a brass pillar from base to bracket, its stems gone woody and ridged at the bottom and still soft and green where they reach the top.
Tillandsias crowd a suspended brass rack in dozens, none of them in soil, their silver rosettes gripping the bars with curved roots and their red flower spikes held at all angles into the humid air.
A pawpaw has seeded itself in the corner drain and rooted there, its trunk already wrist-thick, a ring of unripe green fruits bunched at the base of the leaves directly against the corner glass.
Aerial roots of a monstera have reached the floor of the bed and swollen to the thickness of a man's forearm, each one pale and waxy with a faint green stripe running the full length.
A tree of life aloe has branched at head height into four arms each ending in a stiff rosette, the oldest lower leaves dried to papery brown sheaths still clinging to the trunk below the green.
Passion fruit hangs ripe and purple from the wire trellis overhead, a dozen fruits along one span, one split at its blossom end and showing its amber jelly and the ring of black seeds inside.

Rhododendrons fill the back bed in a solid mass, waxy dark leaves overhead and the lower stems bare and arching, one truss of red flowers fallen onto the path and still perfectly intact on the gravel.
Mangrove roots arc up out of a brackish tank and loop back under, the exposed root-knees standing in a row like blunt wooden pegs, the water below them perfectly dark and still.

A double trunk of Ficus benghalensis has its two stems lashed together with brass wire at three heights and has grown into itself between the wires, the bark bulging in smooth ridges either side of each binding.
Agave leaves lie stacked in a huge flat rosette at floor level, each leaf ending in a rigid black spine, and the outermost leaves have pressed against the bed edging and bent upward along it.
A raised aquatic bed holds floating bladderworts across its whole surface, a solid yellow-flowered mat at one end and clear water showing through at the other where the mat has been pushed back.

A climbing hydrangea has shingled the full height of the end wall, its flat white lacecap flowers pressed against the glass from inside, the woody stems attached directly to the brickwork below the glazing.
Cinnamon bark has peeled from one shrub in the bed and curled into loose scrolls on the soil beneath it, the exposed pale-green new bark on the stem still bright and damp-looking.
A clump of tree dahlias has reached the second catwalk, their hollow square stems braced against the rail with brass clips, each stem tipped with a flat lilac disc still in tight bud.
A rafflesia bud sits in the leaf-litter bed like a mottled rust-red cabbage, its bracts just beginning to separate at the top where the five lobes of the flower will eventually open.

Water hyacinths have blocked the overflow channel, their bulbous petioles packed tight and their lavender flowers standing up in spikes above the mass, the channel behind them backed up several inches deep.
A weeping fig trails its own branchlets in long green curtains from the roof attachment points to the bed below, some strands already rooted in the soil and holding taut, others still hanging loose.
Proteas occupy the driest corner bed, their cone-shaped heads the size of grapefruit, the papery bracts of one fully open head bleached to cream at the tips and still deep pink at the base.
